# Iberian invasion of Cappadocia

}}
The Iberian invasion of Cappadocia was a raid in the 130s AD in which forces of the Kingdom of Iberia under Pharasmanes II,supported by the Alans, entered the Roman province of Cappadocia soon after the ascension of Antoninus Pius to the Roman imperium. The invaders quickly withdrew and left Cappadocia.
Background
The invasion was devastatingly conducted military operation in where Alania and currently Georgia before Kingdom of Iberia in antiquity, were involved. As Flavius Arrianus tells us after his visit in the Caucasus, Pharasmanes II was one of the most influential and powerful kings in the history of Iberia (120–170). Thanks to him, Iberia transformed into a major political player on the international stage. Because of these great achievements and his immense service to the kingdom, Pharasmanes II was given the epithet "the Brave".
Leonti Mroveli tells us:
After 65 BC, when the famous Roman commander Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey the Great) invaded Iberia and Colchis, Iberia was assigned the role of a Roman ally. Naturally, this act of Roman "friendship and alliance" limited Iberia's sovereignty, and the state was considered a vassal of the Roman Empire. Nevertheless, under Roman dominance Iberia achieved certain successes and gradually grew stronger. During the reign of King Pharasmanes II, the situation in Iberia was as described by Leonti Mroveli: a dual kingship existed in the Kingdom of Kartli. King Pharasmanes resided in Armaztsikhe, while King Mithridates sat in Mtskheta. Friendly relations did not exist between the two kings after Mithridates planned to assassinate Pharasmanes and invited him for that purpose. However, Pharasmanes was warned of the danger and thus escaped death. After this, war broke out between Pharasmanes and Mithridates. Pharasmanes emerged victorious, while the defeated Mithridates fled to Parthia. In 125, through his energetic policies, Pharasmanes brought Albania and the weakened Armenia (which at that time had lost its former strength) into his spheres of influence and expanded the territory of the Iberian Kingdom.
Valiant in Mtskheta]]
The era of Pharasmanes' rule coincided with the height of Roman power. Rome was the greatest state of the contemporary world and reached its peak in the 2nd century AD. Rome's main rival in the East was the powerful Parthian Kingdom. Thus, Iberia was surrounded by great states, which naturally posed a serious threat to the kingdom. King Pharasmanes closely observed this situation. In fact, he was positioned between two global powers. Acting under such circumstances was extremely difficult and risky for a kingdom like Iberia in comparison with Rome and Parthia. However, through foresight and prudence, King Pharasmanes correctly assessed the grave challenges facing his kingdom and made swift decisions. The main strategic point of the Caucasus—the Darial Pass—was under King Pharasmanes' control. To the north of Iberia lived the warlike Alans, who represented a formidable force. Pharasmanes decided to open the Darial Pass, bring the warrior Alans south, and together with his own forces unleash them upon the Silk Road. The Alans ravaged Roman and Parthian villages and simultaneously attacked caravans. Laden with great booty, they crossed back through the Darial Pass and returned to their homeland. These raids inflicted enormous damage on the economies of the two great powers—Rome and Parthia. King Pharasmanes made this decision due to the immense pressure coming from these two mighty states. Such active actions by the Iberian ruler severely strained relations between Rome and Iberia and brought them to a critical point. Emperor Hadrian personally traveled to Asia Minor and summoned the kings and rulers of the subordinate states. From the expedition of Flavius Arrianus in 128, we learn that at this time King Pharasmanes also had the tribe of the Dzidritae under his control. The state created by Pharasmanes was by no means a small political entity. Emperor Hadrian demanded that the King of Iberia appear before him.
The Roman historian Aelius Spartianus reports:
Hadrian's attitude toward Pharasmanes can be explained by the active policy that Pharasmanes pursued toward Rome. The King of Iberia accepted the emperor's gifts and, in return, sent Hadrian precious cloaks. However, he firmly refused to appear before the emperor. This precedent indicates that King Pharasmanes was now openly resisting Rome, refusing to declare himself a vassal of the Roman Empire, and fighting for the welfare and sovereignty of his kingdom. Enraged by this, the emperor ordered that the precious cloaks sent by Pharasmanes be placed on 300 gladiators and that they fight each other in the arena. This act was directed as an insult toward the disobedient King of Iberia. Hadrian's behavior created a new rift in Iberian–Roman relations. Upon learning of this audacious act, King Pharasmanes decided to take appropriate measures and demonstrate his great power to the arrogant Hadrian, as well as to Rome and Parthia. In 134–135, Pharasmanes opened the Darial Pass and, together with his cavalry, unleashed the warrior Alans upon the world's main trade artery—the Silk Road. This was the largest and most grandiose attack on the global trade route during the reign of King Pharasmanes. Together with the Georgian cavalry, the Alans invaded the Roman and Parthian states. The united army attacked Albania, Cappadocia, Media, and Armenia. The seriousness of this campaign is demonstrated by the fact that the Parthian king, Vologases II, managed to escape the Alans' devastation only by offering great tribute and gifts.
From this, we can conclude that even a state such as Parthia lacked the strength to stop the Alans. Released onto the Silk Road, the Alans plundered caravans, villages, and cities. This caused colossal economic damage to Rome and Parthia. Eventually, the governor of Cappadocia, Flavius Arrianus, began military preparations, while the Alans withdrew, leaving Rome and Parthia with devastated and plundered provinces. At the head of all this stood King Pharasmanes, who fully demonstrated his capabilities in relations with neighboring states.
Invasion
In 138, the Roman Emperor Hadrian died, and the imperial throne was taken by his adopted son Antoninus Pius. After the death of the arrogant Hadrian, Iberian–Roman relations changed significantly. Antoninus Pius likely realized that Iberia could not be subdued by force, considering that Pharasmanes had at his disposal one of the greatest military forces of the era—the Alans. The emperor pursued a different policy and began peace negotiations. The Roman emperor invited King Pharasmanes to Rome. This was the first time in the history of ancient Iberia that an Iberian king entered Rome at the invitation of an emperor. Pharasmanes accepted the offer, took a large retinue with him for security, and set out for Rome. He entered the capital of the world with pride, where the King of the Iberians was shown unprecedented honor.
The Roman historian Dio Cassius reports:
First of all, Antoninus Pius recognized the sovereignty of Iberia and even expanded its borders for Pharasmanes. He allowed a foreign, non-Roman ruler—the King of the Iberians—to offer sacrifice on the Capitoline Hill, which was an exceptional honor. By the emperor's order, a statue of King Pharasmanes was erected on the Field of Mars. Major events in Rome were recorded on the so-called Fasti. On one such Fasti, discovered at the port of Ostia on the Tiber—among the most important events in Roman history—the visit of Pharasmanes and his family to Rome is listed first. Unfortunately, the names of the king, his son, and his wife have survived only fragmentarily: from the son's name only the final letter "[e]" remains, and from the queen's name only the initial letters "[phr]" (Essays on the History of Georgia, Volume I). With the emergence and strengthening of the Iberian Kingdom on the world stage, Parthia now appeared as its rival. It is worth noting the cycle of military confrontations between Pharasmanes II and the Parthian king Vologases II.
Aftermath
Unfortunately, detailed information about these conflicts has not survived, but we know that Pharasmanes the Brave achieved brilliant victories and significant successes in the war against Parthia. Through this, Pharasmanes II definitively demonstrated his strength. Unable to defeat Pharasmanes through military confrontation, the Parthian royal court decided to treacherously eliminate the King of Iberia. During this period, the conflict between Pharasmanes and Mithridates continued, with the Parthians supporting Mithridates.
According to Leonti Mroveli, the Parthians bribed King Pharasmanes' cook, who poisoned him, causing the death of the great king. Thus died Pharasmanes II, the most powerful king of Iberia, who was granted the epithet "the Brave" by historical fortune. Pharasmanes the Brave was a great ruler, a great military commander, and a great politician. He was a king who managed to rescue his kingdom from a critical situation and bring it onto the world stage. Pharasmanes II will remain in the history of Georgia as one of its strongest kings and leaders, whose legacy time itself cannot diminish.
